edition.alertText: Trump declares Iran war 'effectively over' after meeting Qatar PM at White House — says US 'locked and loaded' but maintaining 'status quo'; Qatar PM brings Iran's $8B Hormuz deal: Iran reopens strait and halts attacks in exchange for lifted blockade and release of frozen funds; Rubio, Bessent, Hegseth reportedly oppose deal terms; Rezaei dismisses Trump's claims as 'FAKE NEWS' about 'imaginary talks'; Iran's Fars News calls deal claims 'mix of truth and lies'; Pezeshkian says Khamenei called for end to 'neither war nor peace'; oil crashes — Brent plunges 5.91% to $92.19, WTI drops 4.41% to $86.37 as deal hopes crush risk premium; gold surges to $4,149 (+1.79%) on haven demand; Dow jumps 1,100 points; UKMTO: Hormuz shipping 'below normal but not stalled' — 170 outbound, 155 inbound transits, ~65% below pre-conflict; JMIC: 177 total incidents since March 1; CENTCOM has redirected 147 vessels, disabled 5; IRGC claims 12 ships caught fire since Nov 1; Iran blacklist reaches 240 vessels; Hormuz Oct crossings at 3-month high (750 total, S&P Global); LNG crossings at 32 in Oct — highest since war began; IMO: 25 seafarers killed, 130+ attacks; ~400 ships with ~6,000 crew still stuck at sea; Trump tells 60 Minutes 'no reason to escalate' — says US has 3 carriers and could destroy 38 bridges in an hour; US gas $4.02/gal (AAA)

situation: The Strait of Hormuz crisis entered day 256 as diplomacy took center stage: President Trump declared the Iran war 'effectively over' after a closed-door meeting with Vice President Vance and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday. Trump said Iran was 'effectively over' militarily, described the current situation as maintaining the 'status quo,' and warned the US was 'locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.' The Qatari PM reportedly brought an Iranian proposal for an interim deal — Iran would reopen Hormuz and halt attacks on Gulf tankers in exchange for the US lifting its naval and economic blockade and releasing approximately $8 billion in Iranian funds frozen in Qatar. Two diplomatic sources told Israeli media that Iran had signed off on the Qatari-brokered terms, though neither government confirmed. Key Trump cabinet members — Treasury Secretary Bessent, Commerce Secretary Lutnick, Secretary of State Rubio, and Defense Secretary Hegseth — reportedly oppose the deal's terms. Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei dismissed Trump's war-over claims as 'FAKE NEWS' about 'imaginary talks,' while Iran's Fars News called the claims a 'mix of truth and lies.' President Pezeshkian told his cabinet that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to the current state of 'neither war nor peace,' saying Iran was 'open to negotiations but will not surrender to force and bullying.' In a 60 Minutes interview airing Sunday, Trump said there was 'no reason' to escalate, claimed the US had suffered no fatalities (the Pentagon's count is 23), and identified 38 bridges he could destroy within an hour. Rubio at the G7 in Paris called Iran's demands 'overblown, ridiculous and really unrealistic' and reported no progress in talks. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Baqaei responded that Washington must end sanctions, the blockade, and the war on all fronts before negotiations can begin.

Oil markets crashed on Monday as the combination of Trump's conciliatory rhetoric and the Qatar-mediated $8 billion deal proposal slashed the war risk premium. Brent crude plunged 5.91% to settle at $92.19/bbl — its lowest since August — while WTI fell 4.41% to $86.37. The move extended a brutal stretch for oil, with Brent now down roughly 21% from its October peak of $117.64. US stocks surged on the oil collapse, with the Dow jumping 1,100 points (+2.15%) and the Nasdaq rising 2.74%. Gold reversed its recent decline, surging 1.79% to $4,149/oz as traders sought haven assets amid uncertainty over whether the deal would actually materialize — Eurasia Group's deal odds remain at just 10%, with a prolonged standoff at 30%. Newcastle coal held steady near $144–145/tonne. Dutch TTF gas eased to around €89.59/MWh ($100.85), down from its four-year high above €101/MWh the prior week, though EU gas storage stood at just 74.33% full versus the five-year average of 86%, leaving Europe exposed heading into winter. The US national average gasoline price held at $4.02/gal (AAA, Nov 8), hovering near the sub-$4 level for the first time since the war began. VLCC rates came under renewed pressure on deal hopes, easing to the $380K–420K/day range for Arabian Gulf–China routes as war-risk premiums softened, down from $420K–460K the prior week. JPMorgan estimated a global crude surplus of 1.4 million barrels/day in October, a headwind that would intensify sharply if Hormuz were to reopen.

The maritime situation remained dangerous despite the diplomatic optimism. UKMTO's weekly report assessed Hormuz shipping as 'below normal but not stalled,' counting 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits — approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. JMIC recorded 177 total incidents since March 1, with five new incidents added in its November 8 update alone. CENTCOM reported that its blockade operations since July had redirected 147 vessels and disabled five that refused to comply, including the M/V Huda and a bulk carrier 18 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan. The IRGC claimed 12 ships had caught fire since the start of November, mostly from naval mines, though UKMTO could independently confirm only 11 attacks in the week ending November 6 — with three vessels sinking. UKMTO has logged 88 projectile strikes since hostilities resumed in July, while acknowledging that most attacks go unreported. Iran's vessel blacklist reached 240 ships for violating its transit guidelines. October Hormuz crossings reached a three-month high of 750 total transits (S&P Global Commodities at Sea), with LNG crossings at 32 — the highest since the war began — suggesting some limited flow normalization even amid sustained attacks. The IMO Secretary-General cited 130 attacks and 25 seafarers killed since the war began, while approximately 400 ships carrying around 6,000 crew remained stuck at sea (DP World). The Mission to Seafarers' happiness index fell for a third consecutive quarter, from 7.18 to 6.81 out of 10.

supplyChain.name: Sulfur
supplyChain.text: Global exports down 39% YoY to 6.1M tonnes in Q2 (S&P). Sulfur prices above $1,000/tonne — more than doubled since pre-war — feeding into phosphate production costs; Egypt, Brazil, India cutting output. Mosaic phosphate plants remain curtailed including South Fort Meade (Florida) — 199 workers laid off. Morocco's OCP needs 3.7M tonnes/yr from the region. Nearly half of seaborne sulfur passed through Hormuz pre-war. Phosphate prices up 25-30%. Trade routes shifting as Morocco and China seek alternative sources (ChemAnalyst).

supplyChain.name: Fertilizer
supplyChain.text: Fertilizer shipments through Hormuz at zero for fourth consecutive month — September, October, and early November all zero (World Visualized/Syz Group/Fertilizer Daily). Urea exports from Hormuz-dependent economies fell 83% YoY in April (ITC). ~850kt urea stranded. 4 of 5 Bangladesh urea plants shut since March due to LNG shortages. Pakistan faces 200,000-ton fertiliser shortfall (Express Tribune). FAO Food Price Index at 136 (highest since Nov 2022). World Bank: fertilizer prices surging as Hormuz disruptions tighten supplies. India building two fertiliser futures — diversifying sources while lobbying for corridor (Diplomat Magazine). Urea-to-corn ratio at 126 bushels/tonne vs 75 in Dec 2025 (CSIS). IFPRI: no bypass route for ammonia or sulfur unlike crude. UN fertilizer corridor stalled pending US-Iran agreement. Fertilizer ships face long backlog even if Hormuz reopens — access not cost will define markets (Supply Chain Brain/World Fertilizer). Out of Hormuz energy shocks, the ingredients for a global food crisis intensify (PRNewswire/IFA).

supplyChain.name: LNG
supplyChain.text: QatarEnergy extends LNG force majeure through end of December 2026 — 8th consecutive extension since April. Global LNG supply gap estimated at ~600 bcf. Dutch TTF gas eased to ~€89.59/MWh (~$100.85), down from 4-year high above €101/MWh prior week; EU gas storage at 74.33% full vs 86% five-year average — lowest in over a decade entering winter (IEA). LNG crossings at Hormuz reached 32 in October — highest since war began (S&P Global). Pakistan to pay >$1B for winter LNG spot cargoes at ~2x Qatari contract price. Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda struck near Hormuz (Oct 31). Bangladesh struggling with spot market costs. Lufthansa says 2026 fuel costs €2B higher amid Iran war. Europe and Asia face tight supply heading into winter. JERA CEO says Qatar LNG supply unlikely to recover soon.

supplyChain.text: MEG ethylene/polyethylene exports disrupted. Gulf petrochem complex cut to ~60% capacity. Methanol down 80% (ITC). Dow, LyondellBasell margins widening on supply constraint. ExxonMobil Q3 profit more than doubled to $15.4B on energy surge. Aramco Q3 profit surges 34.6% to $36.3B.
